profile.summary: Ride-hailing app for 3 cities (~4M people): request, match to a nearby driver, live trip tracking, Stripe card pre-auth at booking and capture at trip end. 8 planned services, all on one shared PostgreSQL schema, Kafka for TripCompleted. Targets: 15k drivers / 120k rides per day at launch, 50k / 400k in year two, Friday peak 4x average, 99.95% availability for requesting a ride, 4 squads of ~6 owning 2 services each. Derived load: ~7,500 GPS UPDATE/s at launch peak (~25,000/s year two); ~6,700 location polls/s at launch peak (~22,000/s year two). Reviewer assumptions (no one available to answer intake questions): card charges must never be lost or doubled; a driver must never be double-matched; location may lag a few seconds; receipts and earnings may lag minutes; each squad ships several times a week; average trip ~20 min; stack Java 17+ / Spring Boot 3.x (user default).
deployables: rider-service (planned): rider profiles, saved payment methods; db=shared ridenow
driver-service (planned): driver profiles, documents, availability; db=shared ridenow; REST callback to matching-service on online/offline
location-service (planned): GPS ping ingest, 'where is driver X'; UPDATE drivers row per ping on shared ridenow
matching-service (planned): nearest available driver; in-memory availability map plus SQL distance query; 1 instance at launch
booking-service (planned): ride lifecycle; sync calls to payment, matching, notification inside one DB transaction; publishes TripCompleted
payment-service (planned): Stripe pre-auth and capture; consumes TripCompleted
datastores: PostgreSQL cluster, single `ridenow` schema, SHARED by all 8 services with cross-service joins
messaging: Kafka topic TripCompleted: producer booking-service; consumers payment-service (capture), receipts, driver earnings

findings.title: Stripe pre-auth, matching and push run inside the booking DB transaction, which cannot roll them back
findings.evidence: "booking-service calls payment-service synchronously, which calls Stripe to pre-authorize the estimated fare. If Stripe is slow, the request waits; we will set a generous timeout so we don't lose bookings." ... "All of steps 2–6 run inside one database transaction in booking-service, so if anything fails the booking is rolled back cleanly."
findings.failure_scenario: (1) The Stripe pre-auth succeeds and matching hands out driver D. (2) notification-service times out, or the booking-service pod is killed by a rolling deploy. (3) The transaction rolls back and the ride row disappears. The Stripe hold stays on the rider's card, D stays marked taken in matching memory, and both may already have had a 'driver on the way' push. (4) The rider taps again, and a second hold is placed. Also: payment-service and matching-service use their own connections, so they cannot see the uncommitted REQUESTED ride row. Any foreign key or lookup they make against it fails or blocks. Under load: each booking holds a Postgres connection and an open xid for the whole Stripe, matching and push round trip. If Stripe stalls for 30 s at Friday peak (~5.6 bookings/s), about 170 connections are pinned in booking-service. That exhausts its pool (trip completion fails too), eats into the shared cluster's max_connections, and holds back vacuum on the hot drivers table.
findings.recommendation: Never hold a DB transaction across a remote call. Commit the ride as REQUESTED in a short transaction. Then drive pre-auth, driver claim and notification as separate steps from persisted ride state, committing each transition (PAYMENT_AUTHORIZED, MATCHED) in its own short transaction. Pass the ride id as the Stripe Idempotency-Key, and pass the data callees need in the request instead of letting them read uncommitted rows. Return 202 with a ride status resource so the app waits on status, not on an open HTTP request. The full state machine is DC-003.
findings.applies_when: Every booking touches money (Stripe hold) and a scarce driver. The brief targets 99.95% for this exact flow, and it runs on a database shared by all eight services.

findings.title: TripCompleted is published after commit with no outbox, so a crash loses the fare capture, receipt and driver earnings
findings.evidence: "booking-service sets the ride to COMPLETED, then publishes a TripCompleted event to Kafka right after the database commit. payment-service consumes it and captures the final fare. Receipts and driver earnings are computed by consumers of the same event."
findings.failure_scenario: (1) The ride commits as COMPLETED. (2) Before the Kafka send is acknowledged, the booking-service pod is restarted (a routine deploy or an eviction), or Kafka is briefly unreachable and the send runs out of retries. (3) No event is ever published. The ride shows COMPLETED, but no capture happens, the Stripe authorization lapses after about 7 days and the fare is lost. The rider gets no receipt and the driver is never credited. Nothing records that the event is missing. At 120k–400k rides a day, a 0.01% loss rate is 12–40 unpaid rides and unpaid drivers every day.
findings.recommendation: Write a TripCompleted row to an outbox table in the same transaction that sets COMPLETED. A relay (polling publisher, or Debezium CDC on the existing Postgres) publishes it keyed by ride id and marks it sent. Consumers must be idempotent, because the relay delivers at least once (DC-006). Add a reconciliation query that flags COMPLETED rides with no capture after N minutes.
findings.applies_when: Fare capture and driver pay depend entirely on this event, and losing a charge is unacceptable. The relay can run on the Postgres and Kafka already planned.

findings.title: matching-service keeps driver availability in instance memory, runs as one instance and starts empty after every restart
findings.evidence: "matching-service keeps the list of available drivers in an in-memory map that driver-service updates through a REST callback whenever a driver goes online or offline. We'll run one matching-service instance at launch and add more later." / "Availability target for requesting a ride: 99.95%."
findings.failure_scenario: (1) The matching squad deploys, or Kubernetes reschedules the only pod. The new process starts with an empty map. Drivers who are already online send no new online/offline callback, so they are invisible. A default readiness probe reports ready, and every POST /bookings finds no driver (and rolls back, per DC-001) until drivers happen to toggle. One such deploy can use up the ~22 minutes a month that 99.95% allows. (2) Callbacks that fail during the restart, or because of any timeout, are never replayed. Drivers whose app died without an 'offline' callback stay in the map as ghosts and keep getting matched. (3) When more replicas are added behind a load balancer, each callback reaches only one replica. The replicas disagree on who is available, and each replica can hand out the same driver (DC-004).
findings.recommendation: Make matching-service stateless. Keep available drivers in a shared store, for example a per-city Redis GEO set fed by location pings and availability events, where a driver drops out when no ping has arrived for N seconds (heartbeat TTL). Every matching replica reads from it. Publish driver-service's online/offline changes as Kafka events (compacted, keyed by driver id) instead of point-to-point REST callbacks, so they can be replayed. Run at least 2 replicas from launch with a PodDisruptionBudget. If any warm-up state remains, gate the readiness probe on it.
findings.applies_when: The service is on the 99.95% ride-request path, squads redeploy several times a week, and year-two load requires more than one instance.

findings.title: The booking flow has no saga state or compensations, and is a synchronous chain across three services and Stripe
findings.evidence: "booking-service: owns the ride lifecycle (requested → matched → in progress → completed)." The steps run through "calls payment-service synchronously", "calls matching-service synchronously" and "calls notification-service synchronously", relying on "if anything fails the booking is rolled back cleanly".
findings.failure_scenario: (a) The pre-auth succeeds but matching finds no driver nearby, which is normal at Friday peak. The rollback removes the ride, but nothing cancels the PaymentIntent, so the rider's funds stay held for days. (b) The matching call times out after a driver was already reserved, and nothing releases the driver. (c) At trip end the capture fails (card declined, or the final fare is above the authorized amount). The ride is COMPLETED with no PAYMENT_FAILED state, retry or dunning path, so the debt is lost silently. (d) Availability multiplies across the chain: booking × payment × Stripe × matching × notification, each at 99.9%, gives about 99.5%, well under the 99.95% target. No persisted state shows how far a ride got, so recovery is manual.
findings.recommendation: Model the ride as a saga orchestrated by booking-service. Persist explicit states, REQUESTED → PAYMENT_AUTHORIZED → DRIVER_RESERVED → MATCHED → IN_PROGRESS → COMPLETED → CAPTURED, plus failure states NO_DRIVER, CANCELLED and PAYMENT_FAILED. Wire compensations: cancel the PaymentIntent on NO_DRIVER or CANCELLED, release the driver reservation on timeout, and retry or escalate PAYMENT_FAILED. Drive the steps through the outbox (DC-002) with idempotent handlers. Run a sweeper that times out rides stuck in intermediate states. The app tracks the ride's status, not a blocking request.
findings.applies_when: The flow has three or more steps with external side effects (a Stripe hold, a driver reservation, a push) that a Postgres rollback cannot undo, and it carries a 99.95% target.

findings.title: Driver assignment is check-then-act on per-instance memory, with no atomic claim in the database
findings.evidence: "matching-service keeps the list of available drivers in an in-memory map ... We'll run one matching-service instance at launch and add more later." ... "matching-service also queries this table to find nearby drivers (`ORDER BY` distance computed in SQL)."
findings.failure_scenario: Two riders on the same block book at the same moment. Both matching requests read driver D as available and both return D. Nothing atomically claims D, so both rides commit MATCHED to D, and both riders get 'driver on the way' because the push goes out before commit. With one instance this can be avoided only if pick-and-remove is synchronized, and the brief does not say it is. Once a second instance is added, double-matching is routine in dense areas at peak. A unique index added later without changing the flow would only fail the second booking at step 6, after its pre-auth and push.
findings.recommendation: Make one store the authority for driver claims, and claim atomically: `UPDATE driver_assignments SET ride_id=?, status='RESERVED', reserved_until=now()+interval '30 seconds' WHERE driver_id=? AND status='AVAILABLE'`, then check that 1 row was affected (or Redis SET NX with a TTL). On 0 rows, try the next candidate. Back it with a partial unique index on rides, `UNIQUE (driver_id) WHERE status IN ('MATCHED','IN_PROGRESS')`. Claim before notifying. The reservation expires unless the saga confirms it (DC-003). Treat the in-memory map and the SQL proximity query as candidate generators only.
findings.applies_when: Concurrent bookings compete for the same nearby drivers at Friday peak, a driver must never be double-matched, and the brief plans to add matching instances.

findings.title: POST /bookings has no idempotency key, so a client retry after the long wait creates a second ride and a second card hold
findings.evidence: "The rider app calls `POST /bookings`." ... "If Stripe is slow, the request waits; we will set a generous timeout so we don't lose bookings."
findings.failure_scenario: Stripe is slow, so the mobile client or api-gateway times out first, or the rider's connection drops and the rider taps 'Request' again. The first request is still running and pre-authorizes and matches driver D1. The retry pre-authorizes again and matches D2. The rider has two card holds and two drivers on the way, one driver's trip is wasted, and support has to void by hand. Retries layered at client, gateway and service multiply the duplicates.
findings.recommendation: The rider app generates a request id per booking attempt and sends it as an Idempotency-Key header. booking-service stores it on the ride row with a unique constraint and returns the existing ride and its status on a repeat request. Combined with the 202-and-status response from DC-001, the client polls the ride instead of re-POSTing. Retry at one layer only.
findings.applies_when: Mobile clients on flaky networks make a long-latency request that has money and driver side effects.

findings.title: TripCompleted consumers (capture, earnings, receipts) are not idempotent, so a redelivery double-counts
findings.evidence: "payment-service consumes it and captures the final fare. Receipts and driver earnings are computed by consumers of the same event." The brief states no delivery guarantee or processed-event tracking.
findings.failure_scenario: Kafka delivers at least once, and once the DC-002 outbox exists, duplicates become routine. The earnings consumer adds a fare to a running total, then rebalances or restarts before committing its offset. On redelivery it adds the fare again and the driver is overpaid. A capture whose response timed out is retried on redelivery. If the final fare differs from the estimate and the difference is charged as a new PaymentIntent, the rider is charged twice. The receipt consumer sends duplicate receipts.
findings.recommendation: Each consumer records processed event ids in a table with a unique (consumer, event_id) constraint, in the same transaction as its effect. Store earnings as per-trip rows unique on ride_id, never as an increment. In payment-service, guard the capture with a status transition (`UPDATE payments SET status='CAPTURING' WHERE ride_id=? AND status='AUTHORIZED'`) and call Stripe with Idempotency-Key = ride id.
findings.applies_when: These consumers move money (capture and driver payouts), and the outbox makes at-least-once delivery an expected case.

findings.title: A "generous" Stripe timeout and no circuit breaker on the booking path let a slow Stripe take down booking
findings.evidence: "If Stripe is slow, the request waits; we will set a generous timeout so we don't lose bookings." The brief states no timeouts for the matching or notification calls, and no circuit breaker anywhere.
findings.failure_scenario: Stripe degrades to 20–30 s responses on a Friday night. Every booking waits the full generous timeout, holding a gateway connection, a booking-service thread, a payment-service thread and (today) a DB connection. Request threads run out in booking-service and payment-service, so trip completion and every other endpoint on those pods queue behind Stripe. While Stripe is fully down, each request still pays the whole timeout before failing, and rider retries (DC-005) add load. A long timeout does not prevent lost bookings. It turns one slow dependency into an outage of the whole ride-request path.
findings.recommendation: Give every outbound client an explicit timeout: connect ~1 s, read from the dependency's p99 with headroom (a few seconds for Stripe), and an overall request deadline. Put a circuit breaker (Resilience4j) around Stripe, matching and notification, failing fast with a clear 'payments unavailable, retrying' state. With the async saga (DC-003), a pre-auth that times out leaves the ride in REQUESTED and is retried with the same idempotency key, so no booking is lost.
findings.applies_when: Stripe is a third party on the 99.95% ride-request path at ~5.6–18.5 bookings/s peak. Provider latency spikes are ordinary events.

findings.title: The 'driver on the way' push is synchronous in the booking flow, so a push or SMS outage fails bookings
findings.evidence: "booking-service calls notification-service synchronously to push "driver on the way" to the rider and the driver." ... "if anything fails the booking is rolled back"
findings.failure_scenario: The push provider (APNs/FCM) or the SMS gateway has an outage or a latency spike, or notification-service is mid-deploy. The call fails. The booking, which had a valid pre-auth and a matched driver, rolls back, so riders cannot get a ride because a notification could not be sent. The rider's response already shows the match, so the push is not needed to answer the request correctly.
findings.recommendation: Take notification off the request path. Commit MATCHED, then emit a RideMatched event through the outbox. notification-service consumes it and retries with backoff out of band. The rider app learns the match from the booking response or status resource, not from the push.
findings.applies_when: Notification is a nice-to-have side effect of a core flow with a 99.95% target, and it depends on third-party push and SMS providers.

findings.title: Live location is written and polled as one row in the shared Postgres, about 7,500 updates/s and 6,700 reads/s at launch peak
findings.evidence: "Drivers' apps send a GPS ping every 2 seconds while online. location-service writes each ping as an `UPDATE drivers SET lat = ?, lng = ? WHERE id = ?` on the shared Postgres. The rider app polls `GET /bookings/{id}/driver-location` every second during a trip, which reads the same row." / "one shared PostgreSQL cluster (one primary, one read replica)" / "Year two: 50,000 active drivers"
findings.failure_scenario: 15,000 drivers / 2 s = 7,500 UPDATE/s at launch peak, and ~25,000/s in year two, all on the one primary that also serves bookings and payments. Each UPDATE writes a new row version plus WAL. Any lat/lng index added for matching stops these being HOT updates, and long booking transactions (DC-001) hold back vacuum, so the drivers table and its indexes bloat. Replica lag grows. Polling adds ~6,700 reads/s (~22,000/s in year two) of the same rows through booking-service pods, the same pods that serve POST /bookings. The writes also contend on driver-service's profile and availability row. At Friday peak, primary IO and WAL saturate and ride requests slow or time out. Year two cannot be met by adding location-service instances, because the bottleneck is the one primary.
findings.recommendation: Move live location out of the relational row. location-service writes the latest position to a per-city Redis GEO set or hash (latest-wins, TTL), and streams raw pings to a Kafka topic keyed by driver_id for trip path and billing distance. Persist to Postgres only at trip milestones. Serve rider tracking from location-service (which the brief already says answers 'where is driver X'), ideally pushed over WebSocket or SSE instead of 1 s polling, and never through booking-service. The same store feeds matching (SC-001, PS-001). Location may lag a few seconds, so none of this changes correctness.
findings.applies_when: The stated peaks (7,500 writes/s at launch, 25,000/s in year two, with a similar read rate) on a single primary that also carries the 99.95% booking path.

findings.title: All eight services share one schema and join each other's tables, so squads cannot change or deploy independently
findings.evidence: "all eight services connect to one shared PostgreSQL cluster (one primary, one read replica) with a single `ridenow` schema. Services can join across each other's tables when they need data, for example booking-service joins `drivers` and `riders` directly to build the trip receipt." / "4 squads of about 6 engineers, each owning two services and shipping independently." / "location-service writes each ping as an `UPDATE drivers ...`"
findings.failure_scenario: The driver-service squad renames or retypes a `drivers` column in its own release. location-service's UPDATE, matching's distance query and booking's receipt join belong to other squads and run old code, and they start failing in production. Even adding a column needs an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on a table taking 7,500 UPDATE/s. The ALTER waits behind in-flight transactions and every later query queues behind it, so location, matching and polling stall together, and another squad's routine deploy becomes a ride-request outage. The `drivers` row has two writers (driver-service for profile and availability, location-service for position), so neither owns its invariants. A full-row ORM save in driver-service can overwrite a fresh position, or the reverse. The brief chose microservices 'so the squads can move independently', and the shared schema removes exactly that.
findings.recommendation: Each service owns its tables and is their only writer. Start with one schema and one DB role per service on the same cluster (cheap), with no cross-schema grants. Replace cross-service joins with API composition for the receipt, or a read model fed by events (booking keeps the driver and rider display fields it needs from DriverUpdated and RiderUpdated events). Move position out of `drivers` entirely (SC-002). Until the split is done, require expand/contract migrations with `lock_timeout`, run as a separate deploy step, with versioned Flyway scripts per owning service.
findings.applies_when: Four squads deploy independently several times a week, and the split into services was made explicitly for that independence. The team size (~24 engineers) justifies the split itself.

findings.title: TripCompleted consumers have no stated retry, dead-letter or ack-after-processing policy
findings.evidence: "payment-service consumes it and captures the final fare. Receipts and driver earnings are computed by consumers of the same event." The brief says nothing about error handling, retries or offset commits.
findings.failure_scenario: The capture for one trip keeps failing (card declined, an unexpected payload, or Stripe 5xx during an outage). With a default Kafka error handler, the record is either retried forever, blocking its partition so every later trip on that partition goes uncaptured and earnings and receipts stop too, or it is skipped after a few attempts, so the fare is silently never captured. With auto-commit on and the capture handed to another thread, a crash after the offset commit loses the capture outright.
findings.recommendation: Commit offsets only after the side effect commits, and process on the listener thread. Add retry topics with backoff, then a dead-letter topic per consumer group, with an alert and a replay tool. Payment failures that are business outcomes (declined) become a PAYMENT_FAILED ride state (DC-003), not a DLQ entry.
findings.applies_when: The consumer moves money and a stuck partition delays captures for thousands of trips. Stripe errors are routine.

findings.title: The nearest-driver query sorts a computed distance over the whole drivers table
findings.evidence: "matching-service also queries this table to find nearby drivers (`ORDER BY` distance computed in SQL)."
findings.failure_scenario: No B-tree index can serve a per-row distance expression, so each match scans and sorts every row of `drivers` (all registered drivers in every city, not only those online), on a table bloated by constant updates (SC-002). The scan runs inside the booking request. Match latency rises with fleet size and the two new cities. At year-two peak (~18.5 bookings/s plus re-matches) it becomes the slowest step of booking.
findings.recommendation: If SC-002 is adopted, answer this from the live-location store (Redis `GEOSEARCH ... BYRADIUS ... COUNT n` on the per-city set of available drivers), and the query goes away. If it stays in Postgres, use PostGIS `geography(Point)` with a GiST index and a KNN `ORDER BY geom <-> :p LIMIT n` query on a narrow location table filtered by city and availability. Do not put that index on the hot profile row.
findings.applies_when: Matching runs on every booking, and the driver table grows from 15k to 50k+ active drivers across five cities.

findings.title: No connection budget or pooler for eight autoscaled services on one Postgres primary
findings.evidence: "all eight services connect to one shared PostgreSQL cluster (one primary, one read replica)" / "How we deploy (probably Kubernetes)."
findings.failure_scenario: With 3 pods per service and HikariCP's default pool of 10, the eight services open about 240 connections, against Postgres's default max_connections of 100. A Friday HPA scale-out, or a rolling deploy that briefly doubles pods, hits 'too many clients' and every service fails to connect at once. Idle-in-transaction connections from the booking flow (DC-001) make it worse.
findings.recommendation: Give each service an explicit pool size, so that the sum over services × max replicas stays below max_connections with headroom. Put PgBouncer in transaction mode in front of the primary. Set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` and statement timeouts. Send read-only queries (receipts, profiles) to the replica on purpose.
findings.applies_when: Eight services likely on Kubernetes with autoscaling, all sharing one primary.

findings.title: No rate limiting or load shedding on the public booking, polling and GPS-ingest paths
findings.evidence: "api-gateway: routing and auth." / "If Stripe is slow, the request waits; we will set a generous timeout"
findings.failure_scenario: When booking slows, rider apps time out and retry while the original requests still hold resources, so load multiplies exactly when capacity drops. After a network blip or a location-service restart, 15,000–50,000 driver apps reconnect at once and flush buffered pings. With no gateway limits, bounded queues or latest-wins coalescing, the burst goes straight to the shared primary and the stall deepens.
findings.recommendation: Add per-client and global rate limits at api-gateway, and bounded concurrency with fast 503s on POST /bookings (safe because of DC-005). Have GPS ingest keep only the latest ping per driver and drop stale ones. Add client backoff with jitter on reconnect.
findings.applies_when: Public mobile clients at 10^4 concurrency on shared infrastructure, with a 99.95% target on booking.

findings.title: Probe design is undecided, and a liveness check on the shared DB would restart all eight services together
findings.evidence: "How we deploy (probably Kubernetes)." / "all eight services connect to one shared PostgreSQL cluster (one primary, one read replica)"
findings.failure_scenario: The Postgres primary fails over or stalls for a few seconds. If liveness is wired to a health endpoint that includes the DB check (a common default when /actuator/health is exposed), every pod of every service fails liveness and Kubernetes restarts them all. The cold starts, the reconnection storm against the recovering primary and the empty matching map (SC-001) turn a seconds-long blip into a minutes-long full outage.
findings.recommendation: Use separate Spring Boot probe groups (`management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled=true`). Liveness checks the process only. Readiness covers the DB and any required warm state, for example the matching availability source. Pair this with PS-002 so a reconnect storm cannot exhaust max_connections.
findings.applies_when: Kubernetes is the likely platform and every service depends on one DB cluster.

findings.title: No distributed tracing across the synchronous booking chain or the Kafka completion flow
findings.evidence: "Observability tooling." is listed under "Not decided yet". Booking spans api-gateway → booking-service → payment-service → Stripe → matching-service → notification-service, and completion fans out over Kafka to three consumers.
findings.failure_scenario: At Friday peak, POST /bookings p99 jumps. The cause could be Stripe, matching's distance scan, the push provider or lock contention in the shared DB. Each squad's logs show only its own hop, with no shared id. When a rider disputes a missing charge, nobody can link the TripCompleted message to the capture attempt. Triage takes hours of cross-squad grepping against a monthly budget of about 22 minutes.
findings.recommendation: Adopt OpenTelemetry (or Micrometer Tracing with an OTel exporter) in every service from the first deploy. Propagate W3C traceparent over HTTP and in Kafka record headers, start traces at api-gateway, and emit structured JSON logs with trace_id and ride_id.
findings.applies_when: Eight deployables, with key flows crossing five of them plus Kafka and two third parties.

findings.title: No metrics, SLO alerting or consumer-lag alerts for the ride-request target or fare capture
findings.evidence: "Availability target for requesting a ride: 99.95%." alongside "Observability tooling." under "Not decided yet"
findings.failure_scenario: payment-service's TripCompleted consumer stalls (a poison message, a Stripe outage or a rebalance loop). Trips keep completing and fares go uncaptured, and nobody notices until finance reconciles days later. Or the match rate falls to zero after a matching restart (SC-001), and riders notice first. Saturation of the shared Postgres builds silently until everything times out at once.
findings.recommendation: Define the ride-request SLI (successful POST /bookings over total) and alert on multi-window SLO burn rate. Collect RED metrics per endpoint and per downstream (Stripe, matching, notification), and USE metrics for DB pools and Postgres. Track business metrics: match rate, time to match, and COMPLETED trips not captured after N minutes. Alert on Kafka consumer lag per group and on DLQ depth (MQ-001). On Spring Boot, the default path is Micrometer, Prometheus and Actuator.
findings.applies_when: The brief commits to 99.95% and money moves asynchronously over Kafka.

findings.title: The TripCompleted contract has no versioning, though three consumers owned by other squads read it
findings.evidence: "publishes a `TripCompleted` event to Kafka ... payment-service consumes it ... Receipts and driver earnings are computed by consumers of the same event." / "each owning two services and shipping independently"
findings.failure_scenario: The booking squad renames `fare` to `finalFare`, or changes the money type from a decimal to integer cents, in its own release. payment-service, owned by another squad and not yet redeployed, fails to deserialize, or reads null and captures 0. Old messages still in the topic cannot be read after the consumer upgrades.
findings.recommendation: Publish a public event type with an explicit version field and tolerant readers, or register the schema (Avro, Protobuf or JSON Schema) with backward-compatibility checks in CI. Never serialize internal entity classes onto the topic, and carry money as integer minor units plus a currency.
findings.applies_when: Producer and consumers belong to different squads that deploy independently, and the payload carries money.

findings.title: No graceful-shutdown plan for in-flight bookings and Kafka consumers during rolling deploys
findings.evidence: "If Stripe is slow, the request waits; we will set a generous timeout" / "How we deploy (probably Kubernetes)."
findings.failure_scenario: A rolling deploy sends SIGTERM while bookings are waiting on Stripe. If the generous timeout is longer than the termination grace period (30 s by default), the pod is killed mid-flow, which produces DC-001's orphaned holds on every deploy at peak. A Kafka consumer killed mid-capture without a clean offset commit causes a redelivery (DC-006). Once DC-001 and RS-001 are fixed, in-flight work is short and this becomes routine hygiene.
findings.recommendation: Set `server.shutdown=graceful` with `spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase` below `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`, add a short preStop delay, and flip readiness to false before draining. Kafka listeners stop polling and commit offsets on shutdown.
findings.applies_when: Squads roll out several times a week on Kubernetes.

findings.title: No plan for config and secrets, and the shared schema implies one DB credential for all services
findings.evidence: "all eight services connect to one shared PostgreSQL cluster ... with a single `ridenow` schema"; payment-service calls Stripe. The brief mentions no config or secrets mechanism.
findings.failure_scenario: If every service uses one `ridenow` login, rotating it after a leak needs a coordinated redeploy of all eight services across four squads. A credential leaked from notification-service grants write access to payment and ride tables. Stripe secret keys with no designated home tend to end up committed in application.yml.
findings.recommendation: Decide now on externalized config (ConfigMaps and env vars) and a secrets manager (Kubernetes Secrets backed by Vault or a cloud secret store). Use one DB role per service (as in SB-001), and keep Stripe keys only in payment-service's secret. A security review should cover this in depth.
findings.applies_when: Before the first deploy, when it is cheap to set up and expensive to retrofit across eight services.

findings.title: The rides table grows by one row per ride, with no partitioning, archival or active-ride index plan
findings.evidence: "Launch: 15,000 active drivers at peak, 120,000 rides per day. Year two: 50,000 active drivers, 400,000 rides per day". The brief mentions no retention, partitioning or indexes.
findings.failure_scenario: rides reaches about 44M rows in year one and about 146M a year after that, on the shared primary. Queries for 'current ride for this rider or driver' that filter on status without a partial index become large scans, and vacuum and index maintenance on one huge heap slow down month by month, on the booking and tracking paths.
findings.recommendation: Partition rides (and payment and earnings records) by month. Add a partial index for active rides (`WHERE status IN ('REQUESTED','MATCHED','IN_PROGRESS')`) and indexes on (rider_id, created_at) and (driver_id, created_at). Archive completed rides older than N months, within finance and legal retention rules.
findings.applies_when: 120k–400k rides a day on one shared primary that must keep ride-request latency low.

strengths: Pre-authorize at booking, capture at trip end: the correct card flow for a fare that is only known after the trip.

Trip completion fans out asynchronously over Kafka to payment, receipts and earnings, so the driver's 'end trip' does not wait on Stripe or on downstream computation. Keep this shape; it needs an outbox and idempotent consumers (DC-002, DC-006), not a redesign.

Service split along business capabilities (rider, driver, location, matching, booking, payment, notification) maps cleanly to 4 squads of ~6 owning two services each, and location ingest has very different scaling needs from profiles. Microservices are justified here; the problem is the shared schema, not the split.
A single edge (api-gateway) for routing and auth is planned from day one.
The brief states concrete, numeric targets (drivers, rides per day, 4x peak factor, 99.95% on the request flow, team shape), which makes proportionate design decisions possible.
